# How to Check a Suspicious Text or Link Before You Forward It

> **In short:** Don't forward, click or reply until you've checked. Look for the warning signs, then confirm the message with the real company or person using contact details you already know are real, not the ones in the message. If it's a scam, report it instead of passing it on. An AI assistant can give you an optional second read, but it can be wrong and it can't tell you who really sent the message.

A message that says "forward this to everyone now!" is pushing you to act fast, and the FTC lists pressure to act immediately as a sign of a scam. Scams also arrive from people you know. This guide gives you a short routine for the moment before you hit send, based on advice from the FTC and CISA. Up front: the official advice we checked covers scams and suspicious links. It doesn't offer a method for judging whether a viral claim is true, so this guide doesn't pretend to.

## Before you start
- The message, left exactly as it is, so you can report it later. Don't tap anything in it.
- A phone number or website you already know is real, for the company or person it mentions.
- An AI assistant is optional. Only Step 5 uses one.

## Step 1 — Pause: don't forward, click or reply
Forwarding passes the message to people who trust you, and links and attachments in a suspicious message can install harmful software on your device. So hold off on all three. The FTC says honest businesses will give you time to decide, so a message that pushes you to act right now is already showing a warning sign.
💬 Example: a text says "Your parcel is on hold. Pay the fee at example.com/pay today and forward this to your friends." Don't tap, don't forward, and keep reading.
You'll know it worked when you haven't tapped, replied or forwarded anything.

## Step 2 — Look for the warning signs
The FTC lists four signs of a scam. The sender pretends to be from an organization you know. They say there's a problem or a prize. They pressure you to act immediately. They insist on a specific way to pay, such as cryptocurrency, a wire transfer, a payment app or gift cards. CISA adds more signs of phishing: urgent or emotional language, requests for personal or financial information, untrusted shortened links, and email addresses or links with small mistakes, like a lookalike address with a swapped letter.

Then ask yourself: "Do I have an account with this company, or do I know this person?" If not, the message could be a phishing scam, so review the signs, report it and delete it.
💬 Example: "There's a problem with your account. Update your payment details right now at example.com/update." It claims a problem, pushes you to act now and asks for payment details: three signs in one short message.
You'll know it worked when you can name the warning signs the message shows.

## Step 3 — If it came from someone you know
A familiar name isn't proof. The FTC says hackers may want to spread malware or scam others, and one sign of a hacked account is friends reporting messages the owner didn't send. So a link or a plea for money that seems to come from a friend may not come from them. If it asks for money, resist the pressure to send it right away, especially by gift card, cryptocurrency, wire transfer or payment app, which are hard to reverse. Contact your friend with a phone number you know is right, or call someone else in your family or circle of friends: a trusted person can help you work out whether the story is true. If you think the account was hacked, tell your friend another way, so they can warn their contacts.
💬 Example: a message from your cousin's chat account says "I'm stuck abroad, send me a gift card code now." Call your cousin on the number you have saved, or ask another relative.
You'll know it worked when you've heard from the real person on a number you chose yourself.

## Step 4 — Check with the real company or person
If the message says it's from a company, contact that company using a phone number or website you know is real: look up the number yourself, or type the website address yourself. Don't use any contact details from the message. If the real company or person says they didn't send it, it's a scam, so go to Step 6. If it was genuine but unexpected, still don't use the links in it. If you can't confirm it, treat it as suspicious and don't forward it.

If the message is a news claim rather than a scam, look for the original report yourself on the publisher's own site, which you type in, instead of trusting the forwarded text. That's common sense rather than an official method.
💬 Example: a message says your bank found a problem. Look up your bank's number yourself, or type its website address, and ask whether there really is a problem.
You'll know it worked when the company or person has confirmed the message, or told you it isn't theirs.

## Step 5 — Optional: ask an AI assistant for a second read
An AI assistant can explain a message's warning signs in plain language, but the official advice doesn't depend on it. Keep four limits in mind:
- It only sees the text you paste in, so it can't confirm who sent the message or whether a link is safe.
- It can be wrong. The makers of these assistants say themselves that answers can be incorrect and should be checked against reliable sources.
- A "this looks fine" answer is never permission to click or forward. Step 4 still applies.
- Services can keep conversations, and some use them to improve their models or let people review them, so check the privacy settings first.

Before you paste, remove names, addresses, phone, account, card and ID numbers, passwords and verification codes, yours and anyone else's.
💬 Example prompt: "Here is a message I received, with personal details removed: [paste here]. Without clicking anything, explain which warning signs of phishing or a scam it shows, if any."
You'll know it worked when the answer points to parts of the message you can see yourself.

## Step 6 — Report it instead of forwarding it, and tell people calmly
The FTC suggests: forward a phishing email to reportphishing@apwg.org; forward a phishing text to 7726 (SPAM); use the report option in your email or messaging app; and report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov. You can also file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. Outside the US, contact your local police or consumer protection agency. Then delete the message.

If you already forwarded it, send the people you passed it to a short, calm note: it may be a scam, so please don't click. There's no need to blame anyone.

If you clicked and then gave away a password, access to your device or money, act quickly. Change the password (and any copy of it) and turn on two-factor authentication, update your security software and run a scan, or, if you paid, contact the company you paid with right away, say it was a scam and ask for a reversal or refund.
You'll know it worked when the message is reported and deleted, and anyone you'd already sent it to has been told.

## Common mistakes
- **Forwarding first and checking later.** Fix: make the pause in Step 1 a habit before you hit send.
- **Trusting a message because a friend sent it.** Their account may have been hacked. Fix: contact them on a number you already know (Step 3).
- **Calling the number in the message to "check".** That puts you in touch with the scammer. Fix: use contact details you already know are real (Step 4).

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** when a text or link makes you want to warn everyone, pause, check it with the real company or person, and report it.
- **For your business or work:** if a message asks you to change payment details or send money, confirm it using contact details you already have.
- **If you want to go further:** share this routine with your family. The FTC says talking things over with someone you trust can help you spot a scam.

## Try it now
Take one message you've been unsure about. Without tapping or forwarding anything, go through the warning signs in Step 2, then check it with the real company or person (Step 4) and report it (Step 6).
